title: Don't let police investigate themselves, says coroner's jury
subtitle: Hearing into death of man shot by police concludes independent body needed
article: A coroner's jury has recommended that police no longer be allowed to investigate their own
officers in cases involving serious injury, assault or death.
The recommendations come after a week-long hearing into the death of Thomas Evon Stevenson, 47, who was shot and killed by two Vancouver police officers after refusing to exit a stolen car.
Stevenson was carrying a replica of a handgun, which officers said he grabbed for just before he was shot.
The jurors also suggested that serious police incidents should be investigated by an independent body, and that specific directions be compiled to guide investigations into police shootings.
Cameron Ward, a lawyer hired to represent Stevenson's family at the inquest, said the jury recognized that police cannot conduct credible investigations of themselves
"Reform of the system is long overdue, and I hope that Solicitor- General \[Rich\] Coleman takes immediate action on this issue," said Ward.
Stevenson's father, Nicholas, lives in Ontario, is in poor health and could not attend the inquest. But he agreed the rules surrounding police internal investigations need to change.
"\[The police department\] never did an investigation," Stevenson said.
No reasons were given for the jurors' recommendations.

Ward said evidence at the inquiry showed there were no fingerprints of value found on the plastic gun. As well, the pathologist who examined the wounds said Stevenson was likely holding his arms outstretched when he was shot.
Investigators made no attempt to reconstruct the scene and never interviewed Sgt. Clive Milligan or Const. Darren Foster, the two officers who fired at Stevenson, Ward told The Province.
"The investigator testified he did not interview any of the police officers involved," he said.
The only account Milligan and Foster gave of their actions on Dec. 7, 2002, was a prepared statement delivered to investigators by their lawyer 17 days later.
Police spokeswoman Const. Sarah Bloor said police officers involved in serious incidents have the same rights as any member of the public and are not obliged to talk to investigators at the scene.
"The officers have the right to legal counsel," she noted.
Const. Tom Stamatakis, president of the Vancouver Police Union, argued that in any investigation, interviewing suspects is not always the top priority for investigators at the scene.
"Your first response is to secure the scene and try to deal with any evidence that you might find." It is also crucial to identify witnesses, he said.
It is not usually necessary to detain police officers for immediate questioning because there is seldom a concern they will flee or pose a danger to the public, Stamatakis added.
Soon after the incident, Milligan, who had been involved in a prior fatality, was transferred to internal affairs. He now teaches the department's use-of-force class.
Bloor said it is up to the provincial solicitor- general to decide who should investigate serious police incidents.

But the jurors' additional recommendations, which include placing video cameras in police vehicles and offering more training for officers, have been sent to the police department's planning and research section for review.
The jurors' recommendations come at a time when the Ontario government is planning to pass a new law that will end the practice of police investigating themselves.
The changes in Ontario were recommended after lawyers and civil rights groups complained that the existing system is biased in favour of the police.
In Vancouver, concern over internal police investigations has been raised in two other fatalities.
A public inquiry into the death of Jeff Berg, who died of injuries during an arrest, is set to begin tomorrow. Civilian witnesses said Berg was attempting to surrender when struck by police.

The police complaint commissioner is also examining the circumstances surrounding the death of Frank Paul, who died of exposure after police dumped him drunk and soaking wet in an alley. In that case, jail guards who helped load Paul into a police wagon said they were never interviewed by internal investigators.
